title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) under adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator. Execution completed all planned pairs (complete_pairs = 200) consuming 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0% on this task bank, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, the preregistered 10% emulator holdout (no validator–emulator disagreements observed), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02).

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with generative language models promises productivity gains but risks producing incorrect or unsafe changes that cause outages or policy violations. Prior work therefore proposes grounding, deterministic validation, and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. The operational benefit of automated repair depends on (i) baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures under the chosen generator/prompting policy, (ii) validator coverage and fidelity, and (iii) the available repair budget and repair‑prompt effectiveness. We preregistered a narrowly scoped confirmatory question: Does an automated, deterministic GVR pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator materially reduce validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only generation pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank? The study used a paired design that fixes the generator output per task and isolates the marginal effect of invoking a validator and, if needed, issuing a single automated repair prompt on that identical candidate.
sections.related_work: Surveys and empirical studies document LLM factual errors, hallucinations, prompt sensitivity, and non‑determinism; mitigation approaches include retrieval grounding, verifier‑assisted repair, and constrained agent architectures. NetOps prototypes demonstrate feasibility of intent→configuration generation but typically lack instrumented, production‑like failure‑rate evaluations. Architectures that combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and guarded agent patterns have been proposed; red‑team audits document configuration‑level brittleness and tool‑description injection vectors that can alter safety outcomes. Our study is an externally auditable, preregistered measurement that isolates the marginal effect of deterministic repair for a fixed model and sampling policy, addressing a gap about when GVR reduces validator‑detectable failures in practice.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The preregistered plan (cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02) fixed a paired design with n = 200 tasks, a single shared deterministic initial generation per task, and a repair budget of at most one automated repair call per task. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline and the primary test an exact two‑sided McNemar test (α = 0.05). Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs used 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). Power planning assumed a baseline unsafe incidence ≈30% and target 50% relative reduction; these assumptions were recorded a priori only to justify sample size.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration task bank with 200 tasks across four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes initial and expected final states plus workflow constraints (make‑before‑break, must_be_down_for_fields, group‑active minima). The primary deterministic checker enforces syntactic and intent/constraint checks and emits structured diagnostics (valid flag, violation codes, parsed_command_count, required_command_count). A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as an independent secondary disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to reveal validator blind spots; the executed contamination check reported no disagreements in that holdout.

Adapter semantics and determinism. The hosted adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced one initial candidate that was reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. This design intentionally removes sampling variance across conditions so the paired comparison isolates the marginal effect of invoking the validator (and, if needed, a single repair) on the identical generator output. Notably, the model configuration artifact records "temperature": null; runtime determinism therefore resulted from adapter enforcement of shared_initial generation semantics (hosted adapter accounting shows a single audited generation per task) rather than from an explicit model temperature parameter set to 0. The audited adapter bookkeeping (referenced artifact: deterministic reconciliation and provider‑call audit fields) documents hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200}, confirming the single shared invocation per task.

Repair policy, budgeting, and handling. The preregistered repair policy allowed at most one automated repair prompt when the primary validator reported violations. Any repaired candidate was re‑validated by the deterministic checker and recorded in validator traces. The execution contract limited maximum model calls to 400 (200 initial + up to 200 repair calls); the adapter enforced this cap. Missingness/exclusion rules deterministically excluded pairs where both conditions failed due to infrastructure execution failures; any task flagged for validator–emulator disagreement would be excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered contamination plan, with deterministic sensitivity analyses preregistered for alternative treatments.

Randomization, seeds, and a documented reproducibility gap. Task ordering and other randomized draws used fixed seeds recorded in the archived task manifest. The preregistered Mininet 10% holdout was executed and reported zero disagreements, but the explicit labeled selection seed identifying which tasks comprised that holdout is not present in the labeled artifacts. We therefore report this missing selection seed as a reproducibility limitation: the contamination summary result (zero disagreements) stands for the executed draw, but exact deterministic reconstruction of that particular holdout draw from the labeled bundle is not possible.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The run completed all planned episodes under the frozen design: completed_episode_count = 400 (shared initial generation reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per task), maximum_model_calls = 400, repair_calls_used = 0. Adapter audit fields confirm hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and single shared_initial_generation stage counts, consistent with the preregistered shared‑initial semantics.

Primary outcomes. Every initial candidate passed the primary deterministic validator: baseline_success_count = 200/200 and guarded_success_count = 200/200. The paired contingency table is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The observed paired difference estimate = 0.0; the exact McNemar two‑sided test yields p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Under the preregistered estimand and test the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis cannot be evaluated because baseline validator failures are absent.

Repair and secondary outcomes. No validator failures occurred, so the preregistered repair branch was never invoked. As a result, preregistered secondary estimands (average repair iterations per repaired task, GVR‑introduced failure rate, model‑call cost per successful repair) have no empirical data in this run and are recorded as unexecuted in the analysis artifacts. The preregistered Mininet holdout (randomized 10%) produced no validator–emulator disagreements as reported in the contamination summary; the previously noted missing selection seed limits bit‑for‑bit reconstruction of that particular draw.

Representative diagnostics. Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count matching required_command_count and validation_after.valid = true on tasks labeled with nontrivial difficulty patterns (labels include "medium", "hard", and "very_hard" with patterns such as make_before_break_uplink_switchover and paired_link_atomic_mtu_change), indicating the task bank exercised substantive dependency constraints despite all outputs passing the checker.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation. The observed null (zero baseline validator failures) is an artifact‑grounded outcome: with n11 = 200 and no discordant pairs the confirmatory test is degenerate (p = 1.0; bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This outcome does not show that repair is categorically useless; rather it shows that, under the tested generation policy and curated workload, there were no validator‑detectable failures for GVR to reduce. The marginal utility of automated repair therefore depends on baseline validator failure prevalence and on validator completeness for the target workload.

Why initial candidates passed. Three archived facts explain the null: the task bank encodes machine‑checkable sequences and workflow constraints that the validator enforces; representative traces show parsed and required command counts matched for many tasks; and the adapter enforced a single deterministic shared‑initial generation per task (removing sampling variance). Together these elements produced validator‑satisfying outputs at scale under the chosen generation policy.

Methodological tradeoffs. The shared_initial paired design was chosen to isolate the incremental effect of invoking validation/repair on a fixed generator output. This internal control sacrifices the ability to measure unconditional failure rates that depend on stochastic sampling: designs that allow independent multi‑sample draws per condition (or nonzero‑temperature sampling) better estimate unconditional operational failure prevalence and the extent to which repair can salvage failing draws. The archived bundle supports alternative analyses in principle, but this confirmatory run intentionally prioritized the paired, shared‑initial contrast.

Validator coverage and emulator corroboration. Deterministic validators are necessary but not sufficient oracles for operational safety. The Mininet emulator was added as a pragmatic secondary check; no disagreements were observed on the executed 10% holdout, but holdout reconstruction is limited by the absent labeled selection seed. Operational assurance therefore benefits from richer validator models, larger emulation samples, and adversarial probing to reveal blind spots.

Implications and future work. For workloads where baseline validator failures are rare under the operational generator/prompt policy, a single‑prompt repair budget yields limited marginal safety returns for validator‑detected errors; resources may be better spent expanding validator fidelity, adversarial testing, or enabling multi‑sample generation. When baseline failures are nontrivial, GVR with an adequate repair budget and well‑designed repair prompts can reduce validator‑detected errors. Future confirmatory studies should (i) include unconditional multi‑sample designs to estimate operational failure rates, (ii) increase repair budgets and allow multi‑step repair or human escalation, (iii) scale emulator checks and record holdout selection seeds for exact reproducibility, and (iv) evaluate multiple models or ensembles to probe model‑dependent brittleness.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic intent/constraint validator. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200; no discordant pairs), resulting in an observed paired difference of 0.0 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). The preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be evaluated because baseline validator failures were absent. This artifact‑grounded outcome emphasizes that GVR’s marginal value is workload dependent: when baseline validator‑detectable failures are rare under the production generator/prompt policy, automated repair yields no measured benefit for those validator‑detected errors. Future studies should target workloads with nontrivial baseline failure rates, expand validator fidelity and emulation checks (with reproducible holdout seeds), evaluate multi‑sample and multi‑model policies, and explore multi‑step or human‑in‑the‑loop repair budgets. All execution artifacts and analysis outputs are archived and documented under the preregistration id cited above.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). Preregistration id: cnsms2026‑gvr‑effectiveness‑02. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses). Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic task generator: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Primary deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI/LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (paired estimand, n = 200, single shared initial generation per task, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair budget = 1 per task) was frozen before any model calls. Execution accounting: the run executed under the frozen plan and used 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were permitted but none were invoked because initial candidates passed the validator. Emulator holdout: a Mininet‑based emulator was preregistered as an independent disagreement detector on a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks); the executed contamination check reported zero disagreements for that holdout. Reproducibility note: the explicit labeled selection seed for the Mininet holdout is not present in the labeled artifacts, preventing exact deterministic reconstruction of the particular holdout draw. Human involvement: the human Research Director provided topic selection and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. No post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested; outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
